newsitem.title: USA: Be it Bosnia or Cyprus, Holbrooke's the man.
newsitem.headline: Be it Bosnia or Cyprus, Holbrooke's the man.

text.p: In the messy puzzle of Balkan politics, it seems that Richard Holbrooke is the only man with the answers.

Holbrooke, the well-known U.S. diplomat who two months ago was named special envoy to Cyprus, was thrust back into Bosnia this week in an effort to rescue his greatest diplomatic achievement: the Dayton peace accords.
And, amid ethnic rivalries that have stumped Europe's best diplomats, Holbrooke once again knocked together a solution.
Holbrooke "is a heavyweight diplomat ... (who) can juggle many balls," the State Department's own spokesman put it, explaining why the 56-year-old New Yorker was sent into action yet again.
Holbrooke posted early success on Friday, resolving a dispute between Bosnia's ethnic leaders over diplomatic posts.
He then leaned on Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic, threatening continued international isolation if he does not fulfil obligations under the Dayton peace acords.
Technically, Holbrooke is not even a part of the U.S. government, having retired in 1996 to take a lucrative job in international banking.

But in times of great diplomatic challenge, the Clinton adminstration seems to turn instinctively to Holbrooke -- a multi-dimensional negotiator who can be erudite and charming one minute, bullying and calculating the next.
Holbrooke, former assistant secretary of state for European and Canadian affairs, was the chief architect of the Balkan peace agreement hammered out in Dayton, Ohio, in 1995.
He was considered for the secretary of state job when President Bill Clinton began his second term in January 1997, but lost out to Madeleine Albright.

A tough negotiator renowned for straight talk, Holbrooke cajoled and bullied the leaders of former Yugoslavia first to enforce a truce in their 43-month-old conflict and then to agree to a map and constitution for a two-part Bosnian state.

His success stood in sharp contrast to the ineffectual attempts by previous mediators to bring peace to the Balkans. Now, with that peace in serious jeopardy, it looks like it is up to Holbrooke once more.

With NATO-led peacekeeping troops, including a large U.S. contingent, due to leave Bosnia next June, there are fears civil war could break out again if the political components of the peace deal are not implemented and adhered to.

Although Washington's new permanent envoy on Bosnia, Robert Gelbard, is well-regarded, officials felt the need to beef up the U.S. team with Holbrooke -- who has achieved a special relationship with Milosevic and other Balkan leaders.

Holbrooke was a reluctant participant in the Balkan turmoil. When he first joined the administration, he told visitors Bosnia was a hopeless case that he planned to have as little to do with as possible.

But he then spotted two developments that he felt opened the way for a new peace bid -- taking advantage of military setbacks for the Serbs and a new U.S. willingness to lead NATO air strikes that put muscle behind Western diplomatic efforts.
Holbrooke has a reputation for not mincing words. He once described Milosevic, the main focus of his negotiating effort, as "not a nice man."

U.S. officials pulled Holbrooke briefly back from retirement last year to make Milosevic force the surrender from power of Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and to help ensure that planned Bosnian elections would not be ruined.

Holbrooke won an agreement in which Karadzic was to stay out of politics, but Karadzic, an indicted war criminal, remains a potent force and U.S. officials consider him a major obstacle to the success of the Dayton accords.
Holbrooke has had easy relations with the media, leading envious colleagues to joke that "the most dangerous place in Bosnia is between Richard Holbrooke and a television camera."
He was U.S. ambassador to Germany from July 1993 until Clinton recalled him to Washington a year later, and has a diplomatic career stretching back to Paris peace talks on the Vietnam war in 1968-69.

Born April 24, 1941 in New York City, Holbrooke joined the foreign service in 1962 after graduating from Brown University. He is married to Kati Marton, an author and former wife of ABC anchor Peter Jennings.
